title: Module Overview: The Defect-One Conjecture
content: The module docstring introduces the Fermat defect-one conjecture: whether $|a^n + b^n - c^n| = 1$ admits a primitive nontrivial solution for every $n \ge 3$. FLT rules out the zero-defect case for $n > 2$; this conjecture asks the natural next question. The Nat-only formulation uses a disjunction `a^n + b^n + 1 = c^n ∨ a^n + b^n = c^n + 1` to avoid signed-integer coercions, keeping the predicates decidable. Both signs of the $n = 3$ benchmark are advertised: $6^3 + 8^3 + 1 = 9^3$ (negative) and $9^3 + 10^3 = 12^3 + 1$ (positive — the Ramanujan-Hardy taxicab number 1729 unit-shifted).
mathContext: Sharp dichotomy at $n \ge 3$: FLT says $a^n + b^n - c^n \ne 0$. The defect-one conjecture says $a^n + b^n - c^n = \pm 1$ is conjecturally always achieved with $\gcd(a, b, c) = 1$.
relatedConcepts: Nat disjunction encoding of absolute value

title: Hierarchy: Levels 0–3
content: The conjecture has a natural ladder of strength. Level 0 (trivial): $a = c, b = 1$ gives $c^n + 1 - c^n = 1$ for any $n$ — pedagogically illustrates why primitivity matters in Diophantine problems. Level 1: nontrivial existence with $2 \le a \le b < c$. Level 2: primitive nontrivial existence (adds $\gcd(a, b, c) = 1$) — this is the headline. Level 3: signed primitive existence, demanding both signs at every $n$. Level 3 may fail at specific $(n, \epsilon)$ due to modular obstructions; a refutation would itself be a result.
mathContext: Level 2 (headline): $\forall n \ge 3,\; \exists a, b, c,\; 2 \le a \le b < c \land \gcd(a, b, c) = 1 \land |a^n + b^n - c^n| = 1$. Level 3 strengthens to per-sign existence.

title: Four Predicates Encoding the Conjecture
content: `FermatDefectWitness n a b c` is the combined predicate: $2 \le a \le b < c$, $\gcd(\gcd(a,b),c) = 1$, and the disjunction $a^n + b^n + 1 = c^n \lor a^n + b^n = c^n + 1$. `FermatDefectExists n := ∃ a b c, FermatDefectWitness n a b c`. The split predicates `FermatDefectPositive n` (only $a^n + b^n = c^n + 1$) and `FermatDefectNegative n` (only $a^n + b^n + 1 = c^n$) isolate each sign for finer-grained Level-3 analysis. All four predicates are `Prop`-valued and decidable on concrete inputs — `decide` and `native_decide` discharge concrete witnesses without algebraic manipulation.
mathContext: Disjunction trick: $|a^n+b^n-c^n| = 1$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ becomes $a^n + b^n + 1 = c^n \lor a^n + b^n = c^n + 1$ on $\mathbb{N}$, decidable for each concrete triple.
relatedConcepts: decidability of Diophantine predicates on Nat

title: Verified n=3 Negative-Defect Benchmark
content: `fermat_defect_three_neg : FermatDefectWitness 3 6 8 9`. Arithmetic: $6^3 = 216$, $8^3 = 512$, $9^3 = 729$, so $216 + 512 + 1 = 729$. Bounds: $2 \le 6 \le 8 < 9$. Primitivity: $\gcd(\gcd(6, 8), 9) = \gcd(2, 9) = 1$. The disjunction is satisfied by the LEFT disjunct ($a^n + b^n + 1 = c^n$, the negative-defect side). Discharged by `native_decide` after refining the conjunction.
mathContext: $6^3 + 8^3 + 1 = 9^3$, i.e., $6^3 + 8^3 - 9^3 = -1$. The negative-defect sibling of the taxicab number 1729 on the other side of $9^3 = 729$.

title: Verified n=3 Positive-Defect Benchmark (Taxicab Shift)
content: `fermat_defect_three_pos : FermatDefectWitness 3 9 10 12`. Arithmetic: $9^3 + 10^3 = 729 + 1000 = 1729 = 1728 + 1 = 12^3 + 1$. Bounds: $2 \le 9 \le 10 < 12$. Primitivity: $\gcd(\gcd(9, 10), 12) = \gcd(1, 12) = 1$. The disjunction is satisfied by the RIGHT disjunct ($a^n + b^n = c^n + 1$, the positive-defect side). Discharged by `native_decide`. This is the Ramanujan-Hardy taxicab number 1729 = 1^3 + 12^3 = 9^3 + 10^3 shifted by one unit — a charming coincidence that makes the n=3 case memorable.
mathContext: $9^3 + 10^3 - 12^3 = 1$. Equivalently $1729 - 12^3 = 1$ — a unit-distance fact about the taxicab number.

title: Derived Existence Theorems at n=3
content: Three corollaries: `fermat_defect_three : FermatDefectExists 3` packages the negative-defect benchmark as defect-one existence. `fermat_defect_three_positive : FermatDefectPositive 3` and `fermat_defect_three_negative : FermatDefectNegative 3` give per-sign existence at n=3, witnessing Level 3 in this case. All three are short consequences of the two benchmarks.
mathContext: Level 3 holds at $n = 3$: both $+1$ and $-1$ defects are realised primitively with $c \le 12$.

title: Headline Open Conjecture (sorry'd)
content: `fermat_defect_one_exists : ∀ n : Nat, 3 ≤ n → FermatDefectExists n`. This is the Level-2 headline statement. It is left as a `sorry` — a genuine open mathematical conjecture, not a placeholder for tractable work. The $n = 3$ case is verified above; $n = 4$ and beyond are open. No general construction is known, and the conjecture is expected to require deep machinery (Pillai-type techniques, possibly abc-style effective forms, or Fermat-Catalan-style modular methods). This is the gallery entry's anchor: an honest research target, marked as such.
mathContext: $\forall n \ge 3,\; \exists a, b, c \in \mathbb{N},\; 2 \le a \le b < c \land \gcd(a, b, c) = 1 \land |a^n + b^n - c^n| = 1$. Status: open for $n \ge 4$.

title: Tactic Pattern: refine + native_decide on Conjunctions
content: Each benchmark's proof obligation is a 5-fold conjunction `2 ≤ a ∧ a ≤ b ∧ b < c ∧ gcd_condition ∧ disjunct`. The proof uses `refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩` to introduce five named goals (one per conjunct), then discharges each with `native_decide`. The disjunct goal is handled with `left; native_decide` (negative defect, $a^n + b^n + 1 = c^n$) or `right; native_decide` (positive defect, $a^n + b^n = c^n + 1$) to pick the correct branch before reducing. This pattern is the canonical Lean 4 idiom for closing concrete-witness goals over decidable predicates: structurally decompose the conjunction, computationally close each leaf. `native_decide` reduces to native-code evaluation (faster than the kernel-level `decide`) and is appropriate here because the arithmetic involves $9^3 = 729$ and $12^3 = 1728$ — large enough that kernel reduction would be slow.
mathContext: Decomposition: $P_1 \land P_2 \land P_3 \land P_4 \land (Q_- \lor Q_+) \;\Leftarrow\; (P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4, Q_\pm)$ with $\pm$ picked by `left`/`right`. All five components are decidable on `Nat`.

title: Imports and Namespace
content: `import Mathlib` pulls in the full Mathlib library — needed for `Nat.gcd`, the `decide`/`native_decide` infrastructure, and standard arithmetic lemmas. The whole file lives in `namespace FermatDefectOne`, so the four predicates and six theorems are exposed as `FermatDefectOne.FermatDefectWitness`, `FermatDefectOne.fermat_defect_three_neg`, etc. Gallery convention: a single `import Mathlib` is preferred over piecemeal imports for self-contained gallery entries; this is distinct from Mathlib-bound files (`mathlib-contribution` skill), which are required to use targeted imports.
mathContext: Namespace prefix: `FermatDefectOne.*` for all exported names. Mathlib provides `Nat.gcd` and decidability instances.

title: GCD-Tower Idiom for Triple Coprimality
content: The primitivity condition `Nat.gcd (Nat.gcd a b) c = 1` encodes coprimality of three naturals via a tower of the binary `Nat.gcd`. Since `Nat.gcd` is binary, the three-argument 'common divisor of $a, b, c$' must be built by composition. Associativity $\gcd(\gcd(a,b),c) = \gcd(a,\gcd(b,c))$ makes the bracketing mathematically irrelevant, but Lean fixes the left-associated form because it matches how the kernel peels the computation: first reduce $\gcd(a,b)$, then reduce against $c$. Concretely: $\gcd(\gcd(6,8),9) = \gcd(2,9) = 1$ and $\gcd(\gcd(9,10),12) = \gcd(1,12) = 1$ — both benchmarks are coprime at the strongest level (the triple shares no common prime factor, not merely no pairwise common factor). Note the distinction: pairwise coprimality is strictly stronger than triple coprimality (e.g., $(6, 10, 15)$ has $\gcd = 1$ overall but $\gcd(6,10) = 2$), so this form admits 'almost-primitive' triples a pairwise condition would reject.
mathContext: $\gcd(\gcd(a, b), c) = 1 \iff \gcd(a, b, c) = 1 \iff a, b, c$ share no common prime factor. Strictly weaker than pairwise coprimality $\gcd(a,b) = \gcd(b,c) = \gcd(a,c) = 1$.

title: Connections to Known Problem Families
content: The defect-one conjecture interpolates between three established families. (1) **Fermat's Last Theorem**: FLT rules out defect 0 for $n > 2$; the defect-one conjecture asks the next question. (2) **Fermat-Catalan** ($x^p + y^q = z^r$, $1/p + 1/q + 1/r < 1$): predicts finitely many primitive solutions. The defect-one problem is a unit-offset slice of the diagonal case $p = q = r = n$. (3) **Pillai-type problems** ($a^x - b^y = c$): for fixed $c$, finitely many solutions; the defect-one problem is morally Pillai on a richer set (sum of two powers vs one power). The verified benchmarks at $n = 3$ also tie into Thue / superelliptic territory once one variable is fixed.
mathContext: FLT (defect 0 forbidden) → defect-one (this conjecture) → Fermat-Catalan (general exponents, finiteness) → Pillai (perfect-power gaps).
prerequisites: exponent vs base structure of $x^p + y^q = z^r$
the notion of primitive Diophantine solutions

title: Mihailescu / Catalan as the Proved Single-Term Defect-One
content: The defect-one equation $a^n + b^n = c^n \pm 1$ has a proved one-term analogue: Catalan's conjecture (1844), now Mihailescu's theorem (2002), states that $x^p - y^q = 1$ with $p, q \ge 2$ has *only* the solution $3^2 - 2^3 = 1$ (i.e., $9 - 8 = 1$). Mihailescu's proof uses cyclotomic-field machinery — primary cyclotomic units, Wieferich-style obstructions on $(p, q)$, Bugeaud-Hanrot annihilator techniques. This is the closest *proved* relative of the present open conjecture, and the toolkit is the modern playbook for perfect-power gap problems. The structural difference is decisive: Catalan-Mihailescu has *one* solution (finitely many), defect-one is conjectured to have at least one solution at *every* $n \ge 3$. A natural research question: do Mihailescu-style cyclotomic obstructions transfer to the two-term diagonal equation $a^n + b^n = c^n \pm 1$?
mathContext: Catalan-Mihailescu: $x^p - y^q = 1$, $p, q \ge 2 \Rightarrow (x, y, p, q) = (3, 2, 2, 3)$. Defect-one: $|a^n + b^n - c^n| = 1$ conjecturally has at least one primitive solution at each $n \ge 3$ — the same '$\pm 1$' on the right-hand side, with two like powers on the left instead of one.
prerequisites: finiteness vs existence in Diophantine settings

title: Structural Hint: Both n=3 Witnesses Share the Number 9
content: The negative-defect witness has $c = 9$ ($6^3 + 8^3 + 1 = 9^3$) and the positive-defect witness has $a = 9$ ($9^3 + 10^3 = 12^3 + 1$). The same integer $9 = 3^2$ appears on opposite sides of $c^n$ in the two benchmarks at $n = 3$. Read against Catalan-Mihailescu, $9 = 3^2$ is the upper member of the unique consecutive-perfect-powers pair $(8, 9) = (2^3, 3^2)$, so $9^3$ is in a sense the smallest cube adjacent to a square that the integer line allows. Whether this is a *structural coincidence* (cubes near small smooth numbers cluster densely) or a *structural hint* (some sign-flipping involution carries one witness to the other through $9^3$) is itself an open question — flagged in the conclusion's `openQuestions` as the 'symmetry between signs' problem. A research-grade probe: does a similar shared-integer phenomenon recur for any other $n$ where both signs are realised? At $n = 3$ the apex is $9$; if a Level-3 witness pair exists at, say, $n = 7$, what is its shared integer (if any)?
mathContext: $\mathrm{neg}\colon\ 6^3 + 8^3 - 9^3 = -1,\quad \mathrm{pos}\colon\ 9^3 + 10^3 - 12^3 = +1$. Both involve $9 = 3^2$. Catalan-Mihailescu: $(8, 9) = (2^3, 3^2)$ are the only consecutive perfect powers $\ge 2$.
